newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Confidence grows over Italy's EMU hopes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Confidence grows over Italy's EMU hopes.

text.p: Confidence over Italy's chances of becoming a founder member of the European single currency gathered momentum on Tuesday, propelling the domestic stock indices and debt markets to record highs.

Ministers and industrialists, often at loggerheads over the past year, for once agreed that Italy's euro prospects were looking good, while the European Economic Affairs Commissioner in Brussels indicated that Rome was on the right track.

Europe's fledgling central bank put the icing on the cake by issuing a bond priced in lira which can be redenominated into euros once the new currency is launched -- signalling that it also believes Italy could make the grade.

Finance Minister Vincenzo Visco told a convention in Rome that the government had tamed the once-tear away public deficit, had inflation under control and was expecting economic output to recover rapidly from a weak first quarter.
"Things can only get better," he said.

Financial markets in Milan showed they were willing to bet on it, with Italian bond and share futures reaching new highs, the Milan blue-chip Mib30 index rising 1.7 percent and the lira powering ahead against the German mark.
"The market's been going up on optimism over a broadly based euro of which Italy is expected to be a member," said Alex Garrard, economist at bank UBS in London."

Prime Minister Romano Prodi has pledged to cut Italy's state deficit to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) this year from 6.7 percent in 1996, thereby fulfilling a key requirement in the Maastricht Treaty for euro aspirants.

Visco said the government was on course to hit the target, but influential industrialists group Confindustria warned that unless interest rates fell, the closely watched ratio would only reach 3.2-3.6 percent.
Despite this, Confindustria said in a report Italy still stood a good chance of joining the euro train when founder members were selected at a European Union summit next May.

"This is especially possible when you consider that probably other major European countries will come forward in May 1998 with 1997 public finances which are not too different from those of Italy," it said.
A year ago Italy was being written-off as a euro no-hoper, with inflation, deficit and debt data all too high.

Since then, inflation has fallen sharply and is expected to be below German levels this month, while the government has introduced some 100 trillion ($60 billion) of deficit cutting measures to bolster state accounts.
And Italy's EMU bid is being helped by difficulties in France and Germany to meet the three percent deficit goal.

European Economic Affairs Commissioner Yves Thibault de Silguy told a group of Italian reporters in Brussels on Tuesday that there was no question of the 3.0 percent deficit criteria being applied too brutally.
He welcomed Italy's recent economic programme for 1998-2000. "The objectives fixed and the areas identified for budgetary reform are good and appropriate," he said.
But he warned that Italy's "moment of truth" regarding qualification for the euro would come in September when it unveils its 1998 budget.

Prodi's centre-left coalition has pledged to introduce an overhaul of the welfare state in the budget to ensure balanced accounts in the years ahead. Negotiations with unions and Confindustria over the planned reform have only just started.
